newsitem.title: USA: US legislator "troubled" by OCC help in fundraiser.
newsitem.headline: US legislator "troubled" by OCC help in fundraiser.

text.p: Rep Spencer Bachus, investigating the Comptroller of the Currency's participation in a May 13 White House fundraising event, said Friday he was disturbed by details of the event disclosed in documents by the comptroller this week.

Comptroller Eugene Ludwig, charged with overseeing U.S. banks, has said he would not have attended the coffee with top bank executives organized by the Democratic National Committee if he had known it was a political event.
Thursday, Ludwig gave the subcommittee chaired by Bachus hundreds of pages of documents concerning the event.

"I am particularly troubled by the extent to which the (Comptroller's Office) was involved in preparing briefing materials and in planning the May 13 political fund-raising event at the White House," Bachus, a Republican from Alabama, said in a statement.
"This is not a trivial matter," Bachus said. "Because it regulates all national banks, the actions of the OCC affect the financial security of every American family."
Bachus also criticized Labor Secretary nominee Alexis Herman for not warning Ludwig about the political event.

Herman, at the time director of the White House Office of Public Liaison, added Ludwig's name to the guest list for the May 13 coffee. Herman has said she did not realize initially that the event was a fund raiser and, once she found out, decided not to attend herself.

"Alexis Herman realized the meeting was improper and did not attend," Bachus said. "Having recognized that fact, as a White House staffer, she should have told Mr. Ludwig that this was a meeting for political fund-raising purposes."
Lee Cross, spokeswoman for the comptroller, also defended the dozens of contacts between Ludwig and top bankers who attended the May 13 event over the subsequent nine months.

"He feels it's very important for him as the head of the office to speak personally and meet with the management of the 25 largest banks at least once a year," Cross said. "In addition, if things come up, he wants to make sure they are aware of it."
Many of the contacts revealed in the documents related to changes in bank regulations in October, November and January, she said.

Bachus, chairman of the House banking subcommittee on general oversight and investigations, said he was not questioning the truthfulness of the Comptroller's statement, adding "there will be no rush judgement."
But Bachus said he had not decided how to proceed.
"Since many questions remain unanswered, I have a personal responsibility to determine what additional action is necessary before this matter can be resolved and will do so," he said.
A spokeswoman for Ludwig reiterated that he would not have participated had he known the nature of the event.

The comptroller also discussed with bank executives pending legislation to reform banking laws. Cross said such contacts did not violate the Anti-Lobbying Act of 1913, as some in Congress have suggested.

The act "does not apply to private communications designed to inform the public of administration positions or to promote those positions," Cross said quoting from a legal opinion written by the Justice Department during the Bush administration.

The opinion adds "there is no restriction on private communications with members of the public so long as there is not a significant expenditure of appropriated funds to solicit pressure on Congress."

At the time of the contacts, Ludwig strongly opposed a bill backed by House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach that would have given primary regulatory authority for financial services companies to the Federal Reserve.
--Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312))
